case: A 1-day-old girl is evaluated in the newborn nursery because of a small head. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation. During the first trimester, her mother lived in a region with ongoing Zika virus transmission and had 4 days of a pruritic maculopapular rash, conjunctival injection, and joint pain. The newborn's head circumference is 29 cm (below the 3rd percentile for gestational age and sex), with overlapping cranial sutures and redundant scalp skin. Her limbs are hypertonic. Head CT shows calcifications at the junction of the cortex and white matter, enlarged lateral ventricles, and a simplified gyral pattern. Zika virus RNA is detected in her serum and urine. The diagnosis is congenital Zika syndrome.

questions.stem: A different newborn also has microcephaly. Examination shows petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly, and the lenses and heart are normal. Head CT shows calcifications lining the lateral ventricles. She fails her newborn hearing screen in both ears. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this newborn's microcephaly?
options: Congenital cytomegalovirus
Congenital toxoplasmosis
Congenital rubella syndrome
Fetal alcohol syndrome
approach: Note where the calcifications are: lining the ventricles, not scattered or at the gray-white junction.
Add petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, and sensorineural hearing loss.
Normal lenses and heart make rubella unlikely, so the pattern fits congenital CMV.
questions.why: Congenital cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital infection. It injures the germinal matrix cells around the ventricles, so calcifications line the ventricles. Petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, and sensorineural hearing loss complete the picture. In congenital Zika syndrome, as in the case patient, calcifications sit mainly at the junction of the cortex and white matter.
whyNot: Correct.
Toxoplasmosis classically causes calcifications scattered through the brain tissue, hydrocephalus, and chorioretinitis. The periventricular pattern with hearing loss points to CMV instead.
Congenital rubella causes sensorineural deafness too, but it also causes cataracts and heart defects such as patent ductus arteriosus, which are absent here.
Fetal alcohol syndrome causes microcephaly with a smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and short palpebral fissures. It does not cause intracranial calcifications, petechiae, or hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.stem: Zika virus is a flavivirus. Its genome can be translated directly by host ribosomes as soon as it enters the cytoplasm. Which of the following neurotropic viruses has the same type of genome but, unlike Zika virus, has no lipid envelope?
options: Rabies virus
Herpes simplex virus
Enterovirus
Measles virus
approach: A genome that works directly as mRNA is positive-sense single-stranded RNA.
Flaviviruses such as Zika and West Nile virus are enveloped positive-sense RNA viruses.
Among neurotropic viruses, the picornaviruses (enteroviruses) are positive-sense but have no envelope.
questions.why: Positive-sense RNA genomes act as mRNA on entry, so the virus needs no packaged polymerase to start making proteins. Enteroviruses, such as coxsackievirus, echovirus, and poliovirus, are positive-sense picornaviruses without an envelope. The lack of an envelope makes them resistant to stomach acid and bile, which fits their fecal-oral spread. They are the most common cause of viral meningitis.
whyNot: Rabies virus is an enveloped, bullet-shaped, negative-sense RNA rhabdovirus. It must carry its own RNA polymerase to make mRNA.
Herpes simplex virus has double-stranded DNA and an envelope. It is the classic cause of temporal lobe encephalitis.
Correct.
Measles virus is an enveloped, negative-sense RNA paramyxovirus. Its persistent brain infection causes subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

topics: RNA viruses of the nervous system

questions.stem: Zika virus is spread by mosquitoes. The mother later moves to the eastern United States, where eastern equine encephalitis virus causes fatal encephalitis in horses and occasionally in humans. Infected horses and humans rarely pass the virus back to mosquitoes. Which of the following best explains how this virus is maintained in nature?
options: Spread among horses by respiratory droplets
Cycling between wild birds and mosquitoes
Latent infection in the nerve ganglia of horses
Persistence in rodent urine and droppings
approach: Horses and humans get sick but do not reinfect mosquitoes, so they are dead-end hosts.
Some other host must reach blood levels high enough to infect feeding mosquitoes.
For eastern and western equine, West Nile, and St. Louis encephalitis viruses, that reservoir is wild birds.
questions.why: Eastern equine encephalitis virus circulates between wild birds and mosquitoes. Birds develop high viremia and infect the mosquitoes that feed on them. Horses and humans reach only low viremia, so they are dead-end hosts, and preventing mosquito bites prevents human cases. Zika virus differs because humans can act as amplifying hosts in an urban cycle with Aedes mosquitoes.
whyNot: Arboviruses are spread by arthropod bites, not respiratory droplets. Droplet spread fits viruses such as influenza or measles.
Correct.
Latency in nerve ganglia is a feature of herpesviruses such as herpes simplex and varicella zoster virus, not arboviruses.
Rodent urine and droppings spread hantavirus and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, not the equine encephalitis viruses.

questions.stem: At 3 years of age, the girl undergoes hearing tests. Bone and air conduction thresholds are equally reduced in both ears, and the loss is greatest at high frequencies. Loss of hair cells in which of the following regions of the cochlea best explains this pattern?
options: Wide, flexible basilar membrane at the apex
Wide, stiff basilar membrane at the base
Narrow, flexible basilar membrane at the apex
Narrow, stiff basilar membrane at the base
approach: Equal bone and air conduction loss means sensorineural loss, so the cochlea or the nerve is at fault.
The basilar membrane is tonotopic: high frequencies peak at the base, low frequencies at the apex.
The base is narrow and stiff, which suits high-frequency vibration.
questions.why: Sound waves travel along the basilar membrane from the oval window toward the helicotrema. Near the base the membrane is narrow and stiff, so it vibrates best at high frequencies. Toward the apex it becomes wide and flexible, which suits low frequencies. Loss of basal hair cells therefore removes high-frequency hearing first, a pattern also seen in age-related hearing loss.
whyNot: The apex is wide and flexible, but it codes low frequencies. Loss there would mainly affect low tones.
The base is stiff but narrow, not wide. The basilar membrane is narrowest and stiffest at the base and widens and softens toward the apex.
The apex is flexible but wide, not narrow. Width increases and stiffness decreases together from base to apex.
Correct.

dx: Temporal lobe ganglioglioma with focal impaired-awareness seizures
case: A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of recurrent spells for 2 years. Each begins with a rising feeling in his stomach and a sense of fear, followed by 1 to 2 minutes of staring, lip smacking, and fumbling with his hands, during which he does not respond. Afterward he is confused for several minutes and cannot recall the event. Neurologic examination between spells is normal. EEG shows spikes over the right anterior temporal region. MRI shows a 2 cm, cortically based, partly cystic mass with a contrast-enhancing nodule and calcification in the right medial temporal lobe, with little surrounding edema. The mass is resected. The diagnosis is ganglioglioma with focal impaired-awareness seizures.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on microscopic examination of the resected mass?
options: Uniform round cells with clear perinuclear halos
Pseudopalisading tumor cells bordering necrosis
Dysplastic ganglion cells mixed with neoplastic glia
Small round blue cells forming Homer Wright rosettes
approach: A slow-growing, cortical, cystic, calcified temporal lobe tumor in a young person with long-standing seizures suggests a low-grade neuronal or mixed neuronal-glial tumor.
The name ganglioglioma means it has both a neuronal (ganglion cell) and a glial component.
Pick the option that contains both cell types.
questions.why: Ganglioglioma contains large, misshapen neurons, sometimes with two nuclei, mixed with neoplastic astrocytes. It is one of the most common tumors found in children and young adults with long-standing temporal lobe epilepsy. It grows slowly, so it causes little edema, and resection often controls the seizures. Central neurocytoma, another neuronal tumor, sits inside the lateral ventricles instead.
whyNot: Uniform round cells with perinuclear halos (a fried-egg look) describe oligodendroglioma, a cerebral hemisphere tumor of adults with IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion.
Pseudopalisading necrosis marks glioblastoma, a fast-growing tumor of older adults with marked edema and mass effect.
Correct.
Homer Wright rosettes of small blue cells are seen in medulloblastoma and neuroblastoma. These are embryonal tumors, not slow-growing cortical tumors.

questions.stem: His spells begin with a sudden sense of fear, which reflects seizure activity in the right amygdala next to the tumor. If both amygdalae were destroyed, as can occur after herpes simplex encephalitis, which of the following would be most likely?
options: Hyperorality, hypersexuality, and placidity
Inability to form new declarative memories
Confabulation with ataxia and ophthalmoplegia
Fluent aphasia with poor comprehension
approach: The amygdala is the limbic center for fear and for the emotional meaning of what we see and touch.
Losing both amygdalae removes fear and the ability to judge objects and partners emotionally.
That combination is Klüver-Bucy syndrome.
questions.why: The amygdala links sensory input to fear and emotional meaning. Bilateral amygdala damage produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome: placid behavior with loss of fear, hyperorality (putting objects in the mouth), and hypersexuality. Herpes simplex encephalitis, which favors the medial temporal lobes, is a classic cause.
whyNot: Correct.
Inability to form new declarative memories (anterograde amnesia) follows bilateral hippocampal damage. The hippocampus lies just behind the amygdala.
Confabulation with ataxia and ophthalmoplegia describes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency, with damage to the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.
Fluent aphasia with poor comprehension follows damage to Wernicke area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, not the amygdala.

questions.stem: Before surgery, he had an episode of status epilepticus lasting 40 minutes. MRI afterward showed swelling of the right hippocampus, followed months later by atrophy of the right hippocampus. Which of the following mechanisms most directly caused this neuronal death?
options: GABA-driven chloride entry through GABA-A receptors
Glycine-driven chloride entry through glycine receptors
Dopamine-driven cAMP rise through D1 receptors
Glutamate-driven calcium entry through NMDA receptors
approach: Prolonged seizures mean sustained excitatory transmission.
The main excitatory transmitter is glutamate, and its NMDA receptors let calcium into the neuron.
Too much intracellular calcium activates destructive enzymes and injures mitochondria, killing the neuron.
questions.why: During long seizures, glutamate floods the synapses. NMDA receptor channels open and let large amounts of calcium into neurons. The calcium activates proteases, phospholipases, and endonucleases and injures mitochondria. This excitotoxic death is the same mechanism that kills neurons around an ischemic stroke.
whyNot: GABA-A receptors let chloride in and hyperpolarize neurons. They limit seizures rather than cause excitotoxic injury, and benzodiazepines enhance them to stop status epilepticus.
Glycine receptors are inhibitory chloride channels, mainly in the brainstem and spinal cord. Glycine is also a coagonist at NMDA receptors, but chloride entry does not cause excitotoxicity.
Dopamine D1 receptors raise cAMP and modulate striatal circuits. They do not cause seizure-related neuron death.
Correct.

questions.stem: In a slice of the resected cortex, a single action potential in one presynaptic neuron produces an excitatory postsynaptic potential that does not trigger firing. When the same presynaptic neuron fires twice within 5 ms, the postsynaptic neuron fires an action potential. Which of the following best explains this result?
options: Spatial summation of EPSPs at the axon hillock
Temporal summation of EPSPs at the axon hillock
Temporal summation of IPSPs at the dendrites
Saltatory conduction along the axon initial segment
approach: One input firing twice in quick succession means summation over time.
Graded EPSPs add when the second arrives before the first has decayed.
If the summed depolarization at the axon hillock reaches threshold, an action potential fires.
questions.why: EPSPs are graded potentials that fade over a few milliseconds. If a second EPSP arrives from the same synapse before the first fades, the two add together. This is temporal summation. The axon hillock has the highest density of voltage-gated sodium channels and the lowest threshold, so it is where summed potentials trigger the action potential.
whyNot: Spatial summation adds EPSPs from different synapses firing at about the same time. Here only one presynaptic neuron was active.
Correct.
IPSPs hyperpolarize the membrane and move it away from threshold, so adding them would prevent firing.
Saltatory conduction is how an action potential jumps between nodes on a myelinated axon. It does not explain how a neuron reaches threshold.

case: An 11-month-old boy is brought to the physician because his parents noticed a white pupil in both eyes in flash photographs. His right eye has also begun to turn inward. His father had one eye removed for a tumor in early childhood. Examination shows absent red reflexes with white pupillary reflexes (leukocoria) in both eyes and esotropia of the right eye. MRI of the orbits shows calcified intraocular masses in both eyes, much larger on the right, with no extension along the optic nerves. Genetic testing shows a heterozygous germline loss-of-function mutation in RB1. The diagnosis is bilateral hereditary retinoblastoma.

questions.stem: After successful treatment of both eyes, he is followed into adulthood. He is at greatest risk of developing which of the following second cancers?
options: Medulloblastoma
Osteosarcoma
Uveal melanoma
Wilms tumor
approach: Bilateral retinoblastoma with a family history means a germline RB1 mutation in every cell.
RB1 normally restrains the G1 to S transition in many tissues, not only the retina.
The classic second cancer in survivors is osteosarcoma, and radiation adds to the risk.
questions.why: Survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma carry one inactivated RB1 allele in all their cells, so other tissues need only one more hit to lose RB function. Osteosarcoma is the classic second tumor. It can arise in bone that received radiation and also in distant bones. Soft tissue sarcomas are also more common, so lifelong follow-up is needed.
whyNot: Medulloblastoma is linked to Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1) and Turcot syndrome (APC), not RB1. The brain tumor linked to hereditary retinoblastoma is a pineal tumor (trilateral retinoblastoma).
Correct.
Uveal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular cancer in adults. It arises from choroidal melanocytes and is not part of the RB1 syndrome.
Wilms tumor is linked to WT1 mutations, as in WAGR and Denys-Drash syndromes, not RB1.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his tumors are bilateral and appeared earlier than the single tumor typical of sporadic retinoblastoma?
options: Inherited activating mutation in one proto-oncogene allele
Somatic loss of both alleles in a single retinal cell
Inherited defect in DNA mismatch repair genes
Inherited loss of one allele; one somatic hit suffices
approach: RB1 is a tumor suppressor, so a cell becomes malignant only when both alleles are lost.
In hereditary cases, every retinal cell already carries one bad allele from the germline.
One somatic hit in any of millions of retinal cells is likely, so tumors arise early, in both eyes, and often at several sites.
questions.why: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis explains this pattern. In hereditary retinoblastoma, the first hit is inherited and present in every cell, so a single somatic mutation in any developing retinal cell produces a tumor. That happens often enough to cause multiple, bilateral tumors in infancy. In sporadic cases, both hits must occur in the same cell, which is rare, so the tumor is usually single and appears later.
whyNot: An activating mutation in one allele is how oncogenes such as RET act. RB1 is a tumor suppressor, so one normal allele still controls the cell cycle.
Somatic loss of both alleles in one cell describes sporadic retinoblastoma, which is usually single, one-sided, and diagnosed later.
Inherited mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome, with colon and endometrial cancers, not retinoblastoma.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before treatment, a swinging flashlight test is done. When the light moves from the left eye to the right eye, both pupils dilate. When it moves back to the left eye, both pupils constrict. Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Reduced afferent input from the right retina
Damage to the right oculomotor nerve
Damage to the right Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Damage to the right ciliary ganglion
approach: Both pupils move together, so the efferent pathways to both eyes work.
Both dilate when the light reaches the right eye, so less light signal reaches the midbrain from that eye.
This is a right relative afferent pupillary defect, from disease of the right retina or optic nerve.
questions.why: Each pretectal nucleus sends input to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so light in either eye normally constricts both pupils equally. When much of the right retina is replaced by tumor, light in the right eye sends a weaker signal than light in the left eye. Swinging from left to right, the drive to constrict drops, so both pupils dilate. This relative afferent pupillary defect points to the retina or optic nerve, not to the efferent pathway.
whyNot: Correct.
A right oculomotor nerve lesion would leave the right pupil dilated and unreactive whichever eye is lit, while the left pupil would still constrict to light in either eye.
Damage to the right Edinger-Westphal nucleus affects the efferent path, so the right pupil would fail to constrict whichever eye is lit, while the left would still respond.
A right ciliary ganglion lesion causes a tonic (Adie) pupil on the right with poor light response, but the left pupil would still constrict normally.

questions.stem: His 15-year-old cousin, who has cystic fibrosis with poorly controlled fat malabsorption, has trouble seeing at dusk and in dim rooms. Her daytime vision is normal. Which of the following components of her rod photoreceptors is most likely depleted?
options: Transducin
Phosphodiesterase 6
Rhodopsin
cGMP-gated sodium channels
approach: Fat malabsorption causes deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamin A.
Vitamin A supplies retinal, which binds opsin to form rhodopsin.
Rods depend on rhodopsin for vision in dim light, so night vision fails first.
questions.why: Rhodopsin is opsin bound to 11-cis retinal, which comes from vitamin A. Light converts 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal, and retinal must be recycled and replenished to rebuild rhodopsin. Without enough vitamin A, rods cannot keep up their rhodopsin, so vision fails in dim light (night blindness). Cone vision is affected later.
whyNot: Transducin is the G protein activated by light-excited rhodopsin. It is a protein made by the rod and does not depend on vitamin A.
Phosphodiesterase 6 breaks down cGMP after transducin activates it. Its supply does not depend on vitamin A.
Correct.
cGMP-gated sodium channels close in light to hyperpolarize the rod. Vitamin A deficiency does not deplete them.

case: A 46-year-old man comes to the physician because of numbness in his left hand for 6 months. He lives in rural Louisiana and often hunts and cleans armadillos. He has been dropping objects from his left hand. Examination shows two well-defined, dry, hairless, hypopigmented plaques on the left forearm that do not sense light touch. The left ulnar nerve is thickened and firm above the medial epicondyle. Sensation is decreased over the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger. A skin biopsy specimen shows well-formed noncaseating granulomas surrounding dermal nerves, and a Fite stain shows rare acid-fast bacilli. The diagnosis is tuberculoid leprosy (Hansen disease) caused by Mycobacterium leprae.

questions.stem: His brother has the same infection but with numerous nodules on the face and ears, thickened facial skin, and symmetric glove-and-stocking sensory loss. Skin smears from the brother show abundant acid-fast bacilli. Which of the following best explains why the patient, unlike his brother, has few bacilli and only localized lesions?
options: Th2 cells secreting IL-4 that suppresses macrophages
Neutralizing IgG that blocks bacterial entry into nerves
Complement-mediated lysis of the waxy bacterial wall
Th1 cells secreting IFN-gamma that activates macrophages
approach: Few bacilli with well-formed granulomas means strong cell-mediated immunity.
Control of intracellular mycobacteria depends on Th1 cells.
IFN-gamma from Th1 cells activates macrophages to kill bacilli and form granulomas.
questions.why: Mycobacterium leprae lives inside macrophages and Schwann cells, so antibodies do little. In tuberculoid leprosy, a strong Th1 response with IL-2 and IFN-gamma activates macrophages, which form tight granulomas and keep bacilli rare. The lesions are few and localized, but the granulomas damage nearby nerves. In lepromatous leprosy, a Th2-dominant response fails to activate macrophages, so bacilli multiply widely, causing leonine facies and symmetric neuropathy.
whyNot: A Th2-dominant response, with IL-4 and IL-10, is what the brother has. It leads to poor macrophage activation and many bacilli in lepromatous leprosy.
Antibodies are made in leprosy, especially the lepromatous form, but they do not reach bacilli inside cells and do not protect.
The waxy mycobacterial cell wall resists complement lysis. Killing depends on activated macrophages.
Correct.

questions.stem: Within the plaques, he also cannot tell a cool metal tube from a warm one. Loss of which of the following receptors and afferent fibers best explains this finding?
options: Pacinian corpuscles of A-beta fibers
Free endings of A-delta and C fibers
Merkel discs of A-beta fibers
Golgi tendon organs of Ib fibers
approach: Temperature sense comes from thermoreceptors.
Thermoreceptors are free nerve endings with no capsule.
Cool travels mainly on thinly myelinated A-delta fibers and warmth on unmyelinated C fibers.
questions.why: Thermoreceptors and nociceptors are free nerve endings in the epidermis and dermis. Cool sensation travels mainly on thin myelinated A-delta fibers, and warmth on unmyelinated C fibers. Mycobacterium leprae favors cool skin and its small dermal nerves, so temperature sense is often among the first sensations lost in the plaques.
whyNot: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting encapsulated receptors in the deep dermis that sense vibration and pressure. They signal on A-beta fibers.
Correct.
Merkel discs are slowly adapting receptors for steady pressure and fine form. They signal on A-beta fibers.
Golgi tendon organs sense muscle tension at the muscle-tendon junction and signal on Ib fibers. They are not skin receptors.

questions.stem: The thickened nerve in this patient is a terminal branch of the brachial plexus. Testing of which of the following movements is most likely to show weakness on his left side?
options: Opposition of the thumb
Extension of the wrist and fingers
Abduction of the fingers
Flexion of the forearm at the elbow
approach: Numbness of the little finger and medial ring finger with a thick nerve at the medial elbow points to the ulnar nerve.
The ulnar nerve comes from the medial cord (C8 and T1) and supplies most intrinsic hand muscles.
The dorsal interossei that spread the fingers are supplied by the ulnar nerve.
questions.why: The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8 and T1). In the hand it supplies the interossei, the medial two lumbricals, the hypothenar muscles, and adductor pollicis. Weak dorsal interossei make finger abduction weak, which adds to his clumsiness. Long-standing ulnar nerve loss causes clawing of the ring and little fingers.
whyNot: Thumb opposition uses the thenar muscles, supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.
Extension of the wrist and fingers is done by forearm extensors supplied by the radial nerve, from the posterior cord.
Correct.
Elbow flexion is done mainly by biceps and brachialis, supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve from the lateral cord.

questions.stem: Granulomas eventually destroy a segment of his ulnar nerve and transect many motor axons. Which of the following changes is most likely to appear in the cell bodies of these motor neurons in the spinal cord over the next 2 weeks?
options: Swollen soma with dispersed Nissl and eccentric nucleus
Shrunken soma with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pyknotic nucleus
Round eosinophilic inclusions of alpha-synuclein in the soma
Neurofibrillary tangles of tau filling the soma
approach: Cutting an axon affects both the distal axon and the cell body.
The distal axon undergoes Wallerian degeneration.
The cell body responds with central chromatolysis as it shifts to making proteins for axon repair.
questions.why: After an axon is cut, the cell body swells, the Nissl substance (rough endoplasmic reticulum) disperses from the center, and the nucleus moves to the edge. This central chromatolysis reflects a shift toward making proteins for axon regrowth and peaks at about 2 weeks. Meanwhile, the axon and myelin distal to the injury break into fragments that macrophages clear, which is Wallerian degeneration.
whyNot: Correct.
A shrunken, eosinophilic cell with a pyknotic nucleus is the red neuron of irreversible ischemic injury, seen 12 to 24 hours after hypoxia.
Alpha-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies) mark Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, not a reaction to axon injury.
Tau neurofibrillary tangles mark Alzheimer disease and other tauopathies, not a reaction to axon injury.

dx: C6 cervical radiculopathy from foraminal osteophytes
case: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of neck pain for 6 weeks that radiates down the lateral side of her right forearm into her thumb and index finger. Turning her head to the right while extending her neck reproduces the arm pain. Muscle strength is 4/5 in right elbow flexion and wrist extension. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the right thumb. Gait and lower limb examination are normal. MRI of the cervical spine shows uncovertebral and facet joint osteophytes narrowing the right C5-C6 intervertebral foramen, with no spinal cord compression. The diagnosis is right C6 radiculopathy from foraminal osteophytes.

questions.stem: If the osteophytes had instead narrowed the right C6-C7 intervertebral foramen, which of the following findings would be most likely?
options: Middle finger numbness with a reduced triceps reflex
Thumb numbness with a reduced brachioradialis reflex
Little finger numbness with weak finger flexion
Lateral shoulder numbness with weak deltoid
approach: Cervical roots exit above the vertebra of the same number, so the C6-C7 foramen carries the C7 root.
C7 supplies sensation to the middle finger and motor fibers to the triceps.
Expect middle finger numbness, triceps weakness, and a reduced triceps reflex.
questions.why: There are eight cervical roots and seven cervical vertebrae. Roots C1 to C7 exit above their vertebrae, and C8 exits between C7 and T1. The C6-C7 foramen therefore holds the C7 root. A C7 radiculopathy, the most common cervical radiculopathy, causes pain and numbness in the middle finger, weak triceps and wrist flexion, and a reduced triceps reflex.
whyNot: Correct.
Thumb numbness with a reduced brachioradialis reflex is the C6 pattern this patient already has, from the C5-C6 foramen.
Little finger numbness with weak finger flexion fits a C8 root lesion at the C7-T1 foramen.
Lateral shoulder numbness with deltoid weakness fits a C5 root lesion at the C4-C5 foramen.

questions.stem: Her right biceps reflex is reduced compared with the left. Which of the following best explains why a root lesion reduces this reflex?
options: Loss of corticospinal inhibition of the alpha motor neurons
Overactive Golgi tendon organ inhibition of the biceps
Loss of Renshaw cell inhibition of the alpha motor neurons
Interruption of the Ia afferent and alpha motor fibers
approach: The biceps reflex is a monosynaptic stretch reflex served by C5 and C6.
Its arc is the muscle spindle, the Ia afferent in the dorsal root, and a direct synapse on the alpha motor neuron, whose axon leaves in the ventral root.
A compressed C6 root carries both limbs of the arc, so the reflex weakens.
questions.why: Tapping the biceps tendon stretches muscle spindles, which fire Ia afferents. These enter the cord in the dorsal root and synapse directly on alpha motor neurons, whose axons leave in the ventral root to contract the biceps. Foraminal osteophytes compress the C6 root in the foramen, where the dorsal and ventral roots run together, so the arc is interrupted. Root and other lower motor neuron lesions lower reflexes, while upper motor neuron lesions raise them.
whyNot: Loss of corticospinal input is an upper motor neuron lesion. It makes reflexes brisk, not reduced.
Golgi tendon organs sense tension and inhibit the same muscle through Ib interneurons. Root compression does not make them overactive.
Loss of Renshaw cell recurrent inhibition would make motor neurons more excitable, so reflexes would rise, not fall.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her husband develops low back pain radiating down the lateral leg. MRI shows nucleus pulposus protruding through a torn annulus fibrosus at L4-L5, just lateral to the midline. Which of the following best explains why lumbar disc herniations usually occur in this posterolateral direction?
options: Anterior longitudinal ligament weakest at its lateral edges
Thin ligamentum flavum over the intervertebral foramina
Narrow posterior longitudinal ligament covering the midline
Nucleus pulposus lying against the anterior annulus
approach: Find the structures that resist backward bulging of the disc.
The posterior longitudinal ligament runs along the backs of the vertebral bodies but is narrow, especially in the lumbar spine.
It reinforces only the midline, so disc material escapes beside it, posterolaterally, toward the nerve roots.
questions.why: The nucleus pulposus sits slightly toward the back of the disc, and the posterior annulus is thinner than the anterior annulus. The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and covers only the midline of the back of the disc. Nucleus pulposus that tears through the annulus therefore usually bulges posterolaterally, beside the ligament, where it presses on the root passing down to the next foramen. At L4-L5, that is the L5 root.
whyNot: The anterior longitudinal ligament is broad and strong and covers the front of the vertebral bodies and discs. Herniation toward the front is uncommon and does not compress roots.
The ligamentum flavum joins the laminae behind the canal. It does not cover the back of the disc and does not direct herniation.
Correct.
The nucleus pulposus lies slightly toward the back of the disc, not against the anterior annulus, which is one reason herniations go backward.

questions.stem: Pain from her right thumb reaches the brain through a specific ascending pathway. Which of the following correctly pairs that pathway with the site where its second-order fibers cross the midline?
options: Spinothalamic tract, caudal medulla
Spinothalamic tract, cord near entry level
Fasciculus cuneatus, cord near entry level
Fasciculus cuneatus, caudal medulla
approach: Pain and temperature travel in the anterolateral (spinothalamic) system.
First-order fibers synapse in the dorsal horn, and second-order fibers cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments.
Touch and vibration from the thumb instead use the fasciculus cuneatus, which crosses in the caudal medulla.
questions.why: Pain fibers from the thumb enter the cord at C6, may travel up or down a segment in Lissauer tract, and synapse in the dorsal horn. Second-order axons cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the opposite spinothalamic tract to the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, then to the somatosensory cortex. A one-sided cord lesion therefore causes pain loss on the opposite side, starting one or two segments below the lesion.
whyNot: The spinothalamic tract does not wait until the medulla to cross. Its second-order fibers cross in the spinal cord close to where the first-order fibers enter.
Correct.
The fasciculus cuneatus carries touch, vibration, and position sense, not pain, and its fibers do not cross in the cord. They ascend on the same side to the medulla.
This is the correct crossing site for the fasciculus cuneatus pathway (as internal arcuate fibers), but that pathway carries touch, vibration, and position sense, not pain.

dx: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar neuropathy at the elbow)
case: A 41-year-old man who spends long hours on the telephone comes to the physician because of numbness and tingling in his right little finger and the medial half of his right ring finger for 3 months. Symptoms worsen when he keeps his elbow bent for long periods and wake him at night when he sleeps with his arms flexed. He has become clumsy when buttoning his shirt. Tapping behind the right medial epicondyle reproduces the tingling, and holding the elbow fully flexed for 1 minute worsens it. Nerve conduction studies show focal slowing of ulnar nerve conduction across the elbow. The diagnosis is right cubital tunnel syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings would best localize his ulnar nerve compression to the elbow rather than to the wrist?
options: Numbness of the palmar little finger
Weakness of the first dorsal interosseous
Numbness of the dorsal ulnar hand
Weakness of the hypothenar muscles
approach: List the ulnar nerve branches that leave the nerve between the elbow and the wrist.
The dorsal cutaneous branch arises in the forearm, above the wrist, and supplies the back of the medial hand.
Numbness in that area means the lesion is above the wrist, as at the cubital tunnel.
questions.why: The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve leaves the main trunk in the distal forearm and does not pass through Guyon canal at the wrist. Compression at the elbow involves it, so the back of the medial hand goes numb, while compression in Guyon canal spares it. Weakness of the ulnar part of flexor digitorum profundus, which flexes the tips of the ring and little fingers, is another sign of a lesion at or above the elbow.
whyNot: The palmar little finger is supplied by the superficial branch that passes through Guyon canal, so it goes numb with compression at either site.
The first dorsal interosseous is supplied by the deep branch in the hand, so it is weak with compression at the elbow or at the wrist.
Correct.
The hypothenar muscles are supplied after the nerve passes through Guyon canal, so they weaken with a lesion at either site.

questions.stem: His 62-year-old sister has received hemodialysis for end-stage kidney disease for 12 years. She has nighttime tingling of both thumbs, index fingers, and middle fingers, with thenar wasting and a positive Phalen sign. Deposition of which of the following proteins in the carpal tunnel is most likely responsible?
options: Transthyretin
Beta-2 microglobulin
Immunoglobulin light chains
Serum amyloid A
approach: Bilateral median nerve symptoms with thenar wasting and a positive Phalen sign mean carpal tunnel syndrome.
Long-term dialysis is a known risk factor because of amyloid deposits.
The amyloid in long-term dialysis is beta-2 microglobulin, which dialysis membranes do not clear well.
questions.why: Beta-2 microglobulin is normally filtered and broken down by the kidneys. In long-term dialysis it builds up in blood and deposits as amyloid in synovium, tendons, and the flexor retinaculum. The deposits narrow the carpal tunnel and compress the median nerve. Other risk factors for carpal tunnel syndrome include pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, and diabetes.
whyNot: Transthyretin amyloid, from aging or inherited mutations, can also cause carpal tunnel syndrome, but long-term dialysis points to beta-2 microglobulin.
Correct.
Light chain (AL) amyloid comes from a plasma cell clone, as in multiple myeloma. Nothing here suggests a plasma cell disorder.
Serum amyloid A (AA) amyloid follows chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis and mainly affects the kidneys, liver, and spleen.

questions.stem: Before nerve conduction studies were done, neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome was also considered, because it can also cause ulnar-side hand paresthesia and intrinsic hand weakness. Which of the following findings would have favored thoracic outlet syndrome over cubital tunnel syndrome?
options: Numbness along the medial forearm
Numbness of the little finger
Weakness of the interossei
Tinel sign at the medial epicondyle
approach: Thoracic outlet syndrome compresses the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8 and T1) above the clavicle.
The lower trunk feeds the ulnar nerve and also the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve to the medial forearm.
Medial forearm numbness cannot come from an ulnar lesion at the elbow, so it points to a higher lesion.
questions.why: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve branches from the medial cord and never passes through the cubital tunnel. A lower trunk lesion, as from a cervical rib or tight scalene muscles, affects both it and the ulnar fibers, so the medial forearm goes numb. Lower trunk lesions can also weaken thenar muscles through their T1 fibers. Arm fatigue, coolness, or pallor with the arm raised suggests that the subclavian vessels are also compressed.
whyNot: Correct.
Little finger numbness occurs in both conditions, because both affect C8 fibers in the ulnar nerve.
Interossei weakness occurs in both, because both affect the ulnar nerve or its C8 and T1 fibers.
A Tinel sign behind the medial epicondyle points to the elbow, which favors cubital tunnel syndrome.

topics: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus

questions.stem: During nerve conduction testing, his ulnar nerve is stimulated twice in a row. A second stimulus 1 ms after the first produces no response at any strength. A second stimulus 3 ms after the first produces a response only if it is stronger than the first. Which of the following best explains the response at 3 ms?
options: Complete Na+ channel inactivation with no K+ efflux
Na+/K+ pump reversal raising the threshold
Calcium channel opening at the nodes of Ranvier
Partial Na+ channel recovery with ongoing K+ efflux
approach: At 1 ms the nerve cannot fire at all, which is the absolute refractory period.
At 3 ms it fires only with a stronger stimulus, which is the relative refractory period.
Some sodium channels have recovered from inactivation, while delayed potassium channels are still open and pull the membrane toward the potassium equilibrium potential.
questions.why: After an action potential, voltage-gated sodium channels stay inactivated until the membrane repolarizes, which sets the absolute refractory period. As they recover, the relative refractory period begins. Fewer sodium channels are available, and the delayed potassium channels are still open, causing afterhyperpolarization. A larger than normal stimulus is needed to reach threshold.
whyNot: Complete sodium channel inactivation defines the absolute refractory period, when no stimulus can trigger a spike. Potassium efflux is high at that time, not absent.
The Na+/K+ ATPase slowly restores ion gradients. It does not reverse, and it does not set the refractory period.
Nodes of Ranvier fire action potentials with voltage-gated sodium channels, not calcium channels.
Correct.

dx: Complex regional pain syndrome type I after a distal radius fracture
case: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of severe burning pain in her right hand 8 weeks after a distal radius fracture was treated with a cast. The pain began while she was in the cast and has spread to the whole hand, beyond any single nerve territory. The touch of a bedsheet is painful. Her right hand is swollen, shiny, and red, and its skin temperature is 1.8 °C (3.2 °F) higher than that of the left hand. Sweating is increased on the right, and finger motion is limited. Nerve conduction studies are normal. X-rays show patchy periarticular osteopenia of the right wrist and hand. The diagnosis is complex regional pain syndrome type I.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if present, would classify her condition as complex regional pain syndrome type II instead?
options: Pain spreading beyond one dermatome
Asymmetric skin color and warmth
Onset after surgery, not fracture
Confirmed injury to a named nerve
approach: Both types share burning pain, allodynia, swelling, and changes in blood flow, sweating, and skin.
Type I follows tissue injury with no definable nerve lesion.
Type II follows injury to an identifiable nerve.
questions.why: Complex regional pain syndrome is divided by whether a major nerve is injured. Type I, the more common form, follows fractures, sprains, or surgery with no definable nerve lesion, as in this patient with normal nerve studies. Type II (once called causalgia) follows a confirmed nerve injury, such as a median nerve laceration. The clinical features are otherwise the same.
whyNot: Pain beyond a single nerve or dermatome is typical of both types and is part of the diagnosis.
Differences in skin color and temperature occur in both types.
Either type can follow surgery or a fracture. The trigger does not decide the type; a nerve injury does.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her sweating and skin changes involve sympathetic fibers to the hand. A local anesthetic is injected around her right stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion. Which of the following best describes the neurons that synapse in this ganglion on their way to the hand?
options: Upper thoracic lateral horn to cells in the ganglion
Lower cervical lateral horn to cells in the ganglion
Brainstem vagal nuclei to cells in the ganglion
Ganglion cells to second neurons within the hand
approach: Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar: preganglionic cell bodies sit in the lateral horn from T1 to L2.
Fibers for the upper limb leave the upper thoracic cord and ascend in the sympathetic chain.
They synapse on postganglionic neurons in chain ganglia, mainly the stellate ganglion, whose axons join the brachial plexus.
questions.why: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons lie in the lateral horn of T1 to L2. Those for the arm come from upper thoracic segments, leave through the ventral roots and white rami, and ascend in the sympathetic chain. They synapse in paravertebral ganglia, especially the stellate ganglion. Long postganglionic fibers then reach the hand through gray rami and the brachial plexus. Parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral, with ganglia near or in the target organ, and does not supply the limbs.
whyNot: Correct.
The cervical cord has no sympathetic lateral horn neurons. Cervical sympathetic ganglia receive preganglionic fibers that ascend from the thoracic cord.
Vagal nuclei are parasympathetic and supply thoracic and abdominal organs. The limbs have no parasympathetic supply.
A second relay near the target is the parasympathetic pattern, with ganglia in or near the organ. Sympathetic postganglionic fibers run all the way from the chain ganglia to the hand.

questions.stem: Her physician explains that the brain normally dampens incoming pain signals. Electrical stimulation of the midbrain periaqueductal gray in experimental animals produces strong pain relief, and naloxone reverses the effect. Which of the following best explains how this stimulation reduces pain?
options: A-beta input exciting inhibitory dorsal horn interneurons
Descending input exciting enkephalin interneurons
Sodium channel blockade along peripheral nociceptor axons
More substance P release onto spinothalamic neurons
approach: Reversal by naloxone means endogenous opioids are involved.
The periaqueductal gray projects to the rostral ventromedial medulla, including the nucleus raphe magnus, which sends fibers down to the dorsal horn.
In the dorsal horn, these fibers excite enkephalin interneurons that inhibit pain transmission.
questions.why: The periaqueductal gray is rich in opioid receptors and drives a descending pathway through the rostral medulla, including the serotonergic nucleus raphe magnus, to the dorsal horn. The descending fibers activate enkephalin-releasing interneurons. Enkephalin acts on opioid receptors to reduce calcium entry into nociceptor terminals and to hyperpolarize projection neurons, so less pain signal reaches the spinothalamic tract. Naloxone blocks the opioid step.
whyNot: A-beta fibers exciting inhibitory interneurons is the gate control mechanism, as when rubbing a painful area. It does not start in the periaqueductal gray.
Correct.
Sodium channel blockade along nociceptor axons is how local anesthetics work, and naloxone would not reverse it.
More substance P release would increase pain transmission, not reduce it.

questions.stem: Norepinephrine released by sympathetic fibers in her hand is partly taken back up into the nerve terminals and partly broken down. Which of the following urinary compounds is the main end product of norepinephrine breakdown by monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase?
options: Homovanillic acid
5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid
Vanillylmandelic acid
Methylmalonic acid
approach: Norepinephrine and epinephrine are broken down by MAO (oxidative deamination) and COMT (O-methylation).
COMT alone produces normetanephrine and metanephrine.
Both enzymes together produce vanillylmandelic acid, the main urinary end product.
questions.why: Norepinephrine and epinephrine are broken down by MAO and COMT, in either order. COMT alone gives normetanephrine and metanephrine, and the two enzymes together give vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). Dopamine follows the same two enzymes to homovanillic acid (HVA). High urinary VMA and HVA help detect neuroblastoma.
whyNot: Homovanillic acid is the end product of dopamine breakdown by the same two enzymes, not of norepinephrine.
5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid comes from serotonin breakdown by MAO and is high in carcinoid syndrome.
Correct.
Methylmalonic acid builds up in vitamin B12 deficiency. It is not a catecholamine metabolite.

dx: Anterior staphylococcal blepharitis with meibomian gland dysfunction
case: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of burning, gritty eyes and morning crusting of his eyelashes for several months. He has facial rosacea. Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination shows red, thickened lid margins with brittle crusts and fibrinous collars around the lash bases. The meibomian gland openings are capped with thick secretions, and pressing on the lids expresses turbid, toothpaste-like material. The tear film is foamy and breaks up quickly. The cornea does not take up fluorescein stain. The diagnosis is anterior staphylococcal blepharitis with meibomian gland dysfunction.

questions.stem: Three weeks later, he develops a painful, red, tender swelling at the margin of his left upper lid, centered on a lash follicle, with a small point of pus. Culture of the pus is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, coagulase-negative
Gram-positive cocci in clusters, coagulase-positive
Gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase-negative
Gram-negative rods, oxidase-positive
approach: A painful, acute swelling pointing with pus at a lash base is an external hordeolum (stye).
A hordeolum is an acute infection of a lid gland, usually by Staphylococcus aureus.
S. aureus is a gram-positive coccus in clusters that is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive.
questions.why: An external hordeolum is an acute abscess of a gland of Zeis or Moll at a lash follicle, and staphylococcal blepharitis raises the risk. Staphylococcus aureus is the usual cause and is identified as gram-positive cocci in clusters that make coagulase. A chalazion, by contrast, is a firm, painless nodule within the lid from a blocked meibomian gland. It is a lipogranuloma, not an infection.
whyNot: Coagulase-negative staphylococci such as Staphylococcus epidermidis are normal lid flora and can colonize blepharitis, but they rarely cause an acute hordeolum.
Correct.
Catalase-negative cocci in chains are streptococci. They are uncommon causes of hordeola.
Oxidase-positive gram-negative rods such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa cause contact lens keratitis, not hordeola.

questions.stem: While cleaning a drain at home, he splashes a sodium hydroxide solution into his right eye. Which of the following best explains why this injury tends to damage deeper eye tissues than an acid splash does?
options: Coagulative necrosis, limited penetration
Caseous necrosis, granuloma formation
Liquefactive necrosis, deep penetration
Fibrinoid necrosis, vessel wall damage
approach: Alkali and acid injure tissue in different ways.
Acids denature and coagulate surface proteins, forming a barrier that slows further spread.
Alkalis saponify membrane lipids and cause liquefactive necrosis, so they keep penetrating into the stroma and anterior chamber.
questions.why: Alkalis such as sodium hydroxide and ammonia saponify the fatty acids of cell membranes, dissolve cells, and cause liquefactive necrosis. With no protein barrier to stop them, they penetrate through the cornea into the anterior chamber and can damage the iris, lens, and trabecular meshwork. Acids coagulate surface proteins, which slows their spread. Immediate, copious irrigation is the first step for any chemical burn.
whyNot: Coagulative necrosis with limited penetration describes an acid burn. It explains why acid usually causes less deep damage.
Caseous necrosis with granulomas is seen in tuberculosis and some fungal infections, not chemical burns.
Correct.
Fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls occurs in vasculitis and malignant hypertension, not chemical eye injury.

questions.stem: In a different patient whose lid margin disease worsened because of poor lid closure, touching the right cornea with a wisp of cotton makes only the left eye blink. Touching the left cornea also makes only the left eye blink. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured, and through which opening does it leave the skull?
options: Right ophthalmic nerve, superior orbital fissure
Left facial nerve, stylomastoid foramen
Right oculomotor nerve, superior orbital fissure
Right facial nerve, stylomastoid foramen
approach: The corneal reflex has a trigeminal (V1) afferent limb and a facial nerve efferent limb, and touching either cornea normally makes both eyes blink.
Touching either cornea makes the left eye blink, so both afferent limbs and the left efferent limb work.
The right eye never blinks, so the right facial nerve is injured. It leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.
questions.why: Touch on the cornea is sensed by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, which enters the skull through the superior orbital fissure. The trigeminal nuclei connect to both facial nuclei, so both eyes blink. The facial nerve closes the eye through orbicularis oculi and leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen. If one eye fails to blink whichever cornea is touched, that eye's facial nerve is damaged, which also explains the poor lid closure.
whyNot: A right ophthalmic nerve lesion would stop both eyes from blinking when the right cornea is touched, while touching the left cornea would make both eyes blink.
A left facial nerve lesion would leave the left eye unable to blink, but the left eye blinks here.
The oculomotor nerve raises the lid through levator palpebrae superioris. It does not close the eye, so it plays no part in the blink.
Correct.

questions.stem: A healthy tear film also needs an adequate aqueous layer. Which of the following ganglia contains the postganglionic neurons that stimulate secretion of this layer?
options: Pterygopalatine ganglion
Ciliary ganglion
Submandibular ganglion
Superior cervical ganglion
approach: The aqueous layer of the tear film comes from the lacrimal gland.
Lacrimal secretion is driven by parasympathetic fibers of the facial nerve that leave in the greater petrosal nerve.
These fibers synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion, and postganglionic fibers reach the gland.
questions.why: The tear film has a lipid layer from the meibomian glands, an aqueous layer from the lacrimal gland, and a mucin layer from conjunctival goblet cells. Lacrimal secretion is driven by facial nerve parasympathetic fibers that leave in the greater petrosal nerve, join the nerve of the pterygoid canal, and synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Postganglionic fibers travel with branches of the maxillary and ophthalmic nerves to the gland. A facial nerve lesion proximal to the geniculate ganglion can therefore cause a dry eye.
whyNot: Correct.
The ciliary ganglion relays oculomotor parasympathetic fibers to the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle, not the lacrimal gland.
The submandibular ganglion relays facial nerve fibers from the chorda tympani to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.
The superior cervical ganglion is sympathetic. Its fibers supply the pupil dilator, the superior tarsal muscle, and blood vessels, and they are not the main drive for tear secretion.

case: A 29-year-old woman who works as a nurse in an outpatient eye clinic comes to the physician because of a red, watery right eye for 5 days. Two days ago her left eye also became red. She had a sore throat the week before, and several coworkers have similar symptoms. Her temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). Examination shows diffuse conjunctival redness with follicles on the inner surface of the lower lids, a watery discharge, and a tender right preauricular lymph node. Ten days later she develops photophobia and blurred vision, and slit-lamp examination shows small, round subepithelial corneal opacities. The diagnosis is adenoviral epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.

questions.stem: Her 24-year-old roommate develops sudden, copious, thick yellow discharge from one eye with marked lid swelling 2 days after sexual contact with a new partner. Gram stain of the discharge is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci
Gram-positive cocci in grapelike clusters
Inclusion bodies in epithelial cells
Eosinophils without any organisms
approach: Viral conjunctivitis is watery with a preauricular node, allergic conjunctivitis itches, and bacterial conjunctivitis is purulent.
Hyperacute, copious purulent discharge after sexual exposure is the classic picture of gonococcal conjunctivitis.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae appears as gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils.
questions.why: Gonococcal conjunctivitis is hyperacute, with heavy purulent discharge and lid swelling that develop within a day or two of exposure. It can perforate the cornea quickly, so it is treated as an emergency. Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils.
whyNot: Correct.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters suggest Staphylococcus aureus, which causes ordinary bacterial conjunctivitis with a milder, slower purulent discharge.
Inclusion bodies in conjunctival epithelial cells mark Chlamydia trachomatis, which causes a follicular conjunctivitis that develops more slowly, over days to weeks.
Eosinophils without organisms suggest allergic conjunctivitis, a type I hypersensitivity reaction with itching and a watery discharge.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who sleeps in his soft contact lenses and rinses them in tap water develops eye pain far worse than his examination suggests. Over several weeks, a ring-shaped infiltrate forms in the corneal stroma. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Acanthamoeba
Herpes simplex virus
Adenovirus
approach: Contact lens wear points to Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba keratitis.
Tap water exposure, a slow course over weeks, pain out of proportion to the findings, and a ring stromal infiltrate favor Acanthamoeba.
Pseudomonas usually causes a rapidly worsening ulcer over a day or two with heavy discharge.
questions.why: Acanthamoeba is a free-living ameba found in tap water, pools, and soil. It contaminates lenses and cases rinsed with water, invades the corneal stroma, and spreads along corneal nerves, which causes pain out of proportion to the findings. A ring-shaped stromal infiltrate develops over weeks. Corneal scrapings or confocal microscopy show cysts and trophozoites.
whyNot: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common cause of contact lens keratitis, but it causes a fast, suppurative ulcer within a day or two, not a slow ring infiltrate with such severe pain.
Correct.
Herpes simplex keratitis causes a branching dendritic epithelial ulcer and is not tied to contact lens care.
Adenovirus causes follicular conjunctivitis with subepithelial opacities, as in the case patient, not a ring stromal infiltrate in a lens wearer.

questions.stem: Her low-grade fever resolves within an hour of taking ibuprofen. Which of the following steps in the fever response does this drug most directly block?
options: Macrophage release of IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha
Sympathetic cholinergic drive to sweat glands
Thyroid hormone release from the thyroid gland
Cyclooxygenase making PGE2 in the hypothalamus
approach: Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) act on the hypothalamus.
They induce cyclooxygenase 2 in endothelial cells near the preoptic area, which makes prostaglandin E2.
PGE2 raises the set point, and ibuprofen blocks cyclooxygenase, so the set point falls back toward normal.
questions.why: Cytokines from infected tissue reach the brain and induce cyclooxygenase 2 in the endothelium around the anterior hypothalamus, especially near the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis. The resulting PGE2 raises the thermoregulatory set point, so the body conserves and makes heat. NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase, PGE2 falls, the set point drops, and the body sheds heat by sweating and vasodilation.
whyNot: NSAIDs do not stop macrophages from releasing IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha. They act further along the pathway, at prostaglandin synthesis.
Sympathetic cholinergic drive to sweat glands helps the body lose heat as a fever breaks. Blocking it would raise temperature, not lower it.
Thyroid hormone sets the basal metabolic rate over days. It is not part of the acute fever pathway, and NSAIDs do not block its release.
Correct.

topics: Fever and the hypothalamic set point

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has floaters and blurred vision in his right eye. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 32/mm3 (reference 500 to 1,500/mm3). Funduscopic examination shows fluffy white retinal infiltrates along the vessels with scattered hemorrhages and little vitreous inflammation. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Toxoplasma gondii
Herpes simplex virus
Cytomegalovirus
Adenovirus
approach: Retinitis with a CD4 count below 50/mm3 suggests an opportunistic infection.
White infiltrates along the vessels with hemorrhages and little vitreous inflammation are classic for CMV retinitis.
Toxoplasma chorioretinitis instead causes focal lesions with dense vitreous inflammation.
questions.why: Cytomegalovirus retinitis occurs mostly when the CD4 count falls below 50/mm3. It spreads along the vessels as white, necrotic retina with hemorrhages. Vitreous inflammation is mild because the immune response is weak. Untreated, it destroys the retina and can lead to retinal detachment and blindness.
whyNot: Toxoplasma gondii causes a focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis, often next to an old scar, with marked vitreous haze. It is the most common infectious cause of posterior uveitis in people with normal immunity.
Herpes simplex and varicella zoster viruses can cause acute retinal necrosis, but it begins in the peripheral retina with marked inflammation, and CMV is far more common at this CD4 count.
Correct.
Adenovirus infects the conjunctiva and cornea, as in the case patient. It does not cause retinitis.

case: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of swelling around his left eye for 2 days. He had a cold with nasal congestion for 1 week. His temperature is 39.2 °C (102.6 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. The left upper and lower lids are red and swollen. The left eye bulges forward, moving it is painful, and upward and lateral gaze are limited, causing double vision. Visual acuity is 20/20 on the right and 20/30 on the left. Leukocyte count is 17,800/mm3 (reference 4,500 to 11,000/mm3). CT shows opacified left ethmoid air cells and inflammation of the orbital fat behind the orbital septum, with a small abscess along the medial orbital wall. The diagnosis is orbital cellulitis from ethmoid sinusitis.

questions.stem: His 4-year-old sister has red, swollen eyelids on one side after an insect bite. Her eye movements are full and painless, her vision is normal, and there is no proptosis. Which of the following structures most likely confines her infection to the eyelids?
options: Lamina papyracea
Tenon capsule
Orbital septum
Common tendinous ring
approach: Lid swelling without painful eye movement, proptosis, or vision loss means preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis.
The orbital septum, a fibrous sheet running from the orbital rim into the lids, divides the lids from the orbit.
Infection in front of it stays in the lids, and infection behind it involves orbital fat and muscles.
questions.why: The orbital septum extends from the periosteum of the orbital rim to the tarsal plates. Preseptal cellulitis, often after a bite, scratch, or lid lesion, stays in front of it, so eye movements, vision, and the position of the globe are normal. Orbital cellulitis lies behind the septum and causes painful eye movement, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and sometimes vision loss, as in her brother.
whyNot: The lamina papyracea is the thin medial orbital wall. It is the route by which ethmoid infection reaches the orbit, as in her brother, not a barrier for lid infection.
Tenon capsule is the fascial sheath around the globe inside the orbit. It lies behind the septum.
Correct.
The common tendinous ring at the orbital apex anchors the rectus muscles. It does not separate the lids from the orbit.

questions.stem: Two days later, despite treatment, both eyes bulge, the right eye cannot move laterally, and sensation is reduced over the forehead on both sides. Spread of infection by which of the following routes most likely explains these new findings?
options: Emissary veins into the superior sagittal sinus
Pterygoid plexus into the sigmoid sinus
Bridging veins into the transverse sinus
Ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus
approach: New bilateral proptosis with palsies of cranial nerves VI and V1 points to the cavernous sinus.
Orbital veins drain through the valveless superior and inferior ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus.
The two cavernous sinuses connect across the midline, so infection and clot can spread to the other side.
questions.why: The ophthalmic veins have no valves and drain the orbit and upper face into the cavernous sinus. Infection can spread back along them and cause septic cavernous sinus thrombosis. Cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI run in or beside the sinus, and VI, which lies free within it next to the internal carotid artery, is often affected first. Intercavernous connections let the clot spread to the other side, and blocked venous outflow can raise intracranial pressure.
whyNot: Emissary veins link scalp veins to the superior sagittal sinus. Thrombosis there raises intracranial pressure and can cause hemorrhagic venous infarcts, but not orbital signs or abducens palsy.
The pterygoid plexus connects the deep face to the cavernous sinus, not to the sigmoid sinus, which drains into the internal jugular vein.
Bridging veins cross from the cortex to the dural sinuses. Tearing them causes subdural hematoma, and they do not drain the orbit.
Correct.

questions.stem: Culture of the drained abscess grows alpha-hemolytic, lancet-shaped, gram-positive diplococci that dissolve in bile and are inhibited by optochin. Which of the following is the main virulence factor that lets this organism avoid phagocytosis?
options: Polysaccharide capsule
Lipooligosaccharide endotoxin
Protein A binding IgG Fc
M protein blocking complement
approach: Alpha-hemolytic, lancet-shaped diplococci that are bile soluble and optochin sensitive are Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Its key virulence factor is the polysaccharide capsule.
The capsule blocks complement deposition and phagocytosis unless anticapsular antibody opsonizes it.
questions.why: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of sinusitis, otitis media, pneumonia, and meningitis. Its polysaccharide capsule shields it from complement and phagocytes, and about 100 serotypes differ in capsule structure. Opsonizing antibody to the capsule and a working spleen are the main defenses, so people without a spleen are at high risk.
whyNot: Correct.
Lipooligosaccharide endotoxin is an outer membrane component of gram-negative bacteria and a major virulence factor of Neisseria meningitidis. Pneumococci are gram-positive and have no endotoxin.
Protein A binds the Fc portion of IgG and belongs to Staphylococcus aureus, a gram-positive coccus in clusters.
M protein is the antiphagocytic surface protein of Streptococcus pyogenes, a beta-hemolytic coccus in chains.

questions.stem: His family recently immigrated, and his records show that he received oral live attenuated polio vaccine as an infant. Compared with the injected inactivated polio vaccine, which of the following is the main immunologic advantage of the oral vaccine?
options: Lower risk of vaccine-derived paralysis
Greater gut mucosal IgA response
Safer use in immunodeficient contacts
Response that bypasses helper T cells
approach: The oral vaccine is a live virus that replicates in the intestine, much like natural infection.
Replication in gut lymphoid tissue induces secretory IgA at the mucosa as well as serum IgG.
Mucosal IgA blocks intestinal infection and shedding, which interrupts spread in a community.
questions.why: The oral (Sabin) vaccine contains live attenuated virus that replicates in the gut, so it induces secretory IgA in the intestinal mucosa along with serum IgG. Mucosal IgA limits viral replication and fecal shedding, which helps stop community spread. The injected inactivated (Salk) vaccine induces strong serum IgG that keeps the virus from reaching the nervous system, but weaker gut immunity. Because the live virus can rarely revert and cause paralysis, the United States uses only the inactivated vaccine.
whyNot: Lower risk of vaccine-derived paralysis is an advantage of the inactivated vaccine. The live oral virus can rarely revert to a form that paralyzes.
Correct.
The oral vaccine is less safe for people with immunodeficiency and their household contacts, because the live virus is shed in stool.
Both polio vaccines contain protein antigens that recruit helper T cells. T cell-independent responses are typical of plain polysaccharide vaccines, which is why conjugate vaccines were developed.
